fetched_contents.text: Selective adsorption of heavy metal ions by different composite-modified semi-carbonized fibers Introduction The heavy metal industry has entered a period of rapid development with the increasing progress of industrial and agricultural technology [1]. However, this growth has also caused heavy metal pollution and environmental crisis. If industrial wastes are discharged without treatment, then they will pollute and degrade not only groundwater, lakes, and soil quality but also reduce crops [2]. Various pollutants in the water environment often exist simultaneously in some countries due to the insufficient combustion of petrochemical products and chemical fuels as well as long-term sewage irrigation, among which heavy metal pollution is a common phenomenon in water environment pollution [3], [4]. Therefore, pollution control and wastewater treatment are primarily considered in this field of environmental research [5]. Hence, developing a convenient and effective method for removing heavy metals from wastewater is urgently necessary. Existing studies have shown that physical, chemical, and biological remediation strategies are often used to remove heavy metal from wastewater [6]. Among them, the main methods are coagulation sedimentation, electrodialysis, reverse osmosis, electric flocculation, and adsorption. The adsorption method is widely used in the treatment of harmful heavy metals because of its satisfactory treatment effect and simple operation process [7]. Different materials present varying adsorption effects on heavy metals in water, and structural and functional groups of material are key factors in determining the adsorption effects of heavy metals [8]. Common adsorption materials include active alumina, activated carbon, diatomite, and spherical resin. Although conventional adsorption materials are limited by their large consumption and high cost, the use of modifying agents is often highly convenient, economical, and efficient [9]. Zhong et al. revealed that wheat straw altered with an amphoteric modifier presents high adsorption ability for heavy metals, with a maximum adsorption capacity for Cu(II) and Cr(VI) of 90.9 and 241.1 mg g−1, respectively [10]. The adsorption amounts of Cd(II) and Cr(VI) with bentonite altered with cationic, anionic, and amphoteric modifiers increase several times more than those of unmodified bentonite [11]. Surface modifiers can improve the adsorption performance of clay to heavy metals, and amphoteric modification is favorable to clay for the adsorption of heavy metals [12]. Carbon fiber, a solid carbon-rich substance made by burning natural or synthetic polymer compounds, is obtained from a wide range of sources [13]. This material has been widely used in sewage treatment, soil remediation, and other aspects because of its developed pore structure and large adsorption capacity [14]. Biochar prepared with chemical and plant fibers as raw materials is widely used in the environmental field because it can reduce not only the cost of activated carbon but also realize the comprehensive utilization of high value through combustion, gasification, pyrolysis, and other ways [15]. These basic characteristics increase the adsorption capacity of activated carbon prepared from plant and chemical fibers for inorganic pollutants in environmental media. At present, the use of carbon fiber to treat polluted water has achieved a high removal rate of various pollutants. Wu et al. revealed that the adsorption equilibrium of Cu(II) using chitosan-based electrospun nanofibrous membranes is established within 120 min with a maximum Cu(II) adsorption capacity of 90.3 mg g−1 [16]. The Cu(II) removal performance of the treated coconut coir samples was almost five times higher than that of raw coconut coir under optimized conditions [17]. Razak et al. met with actual wastewater substrates from electroplating (88.2% removal rate) and wood treatment (61.5% removal rate) industries and demonstrated that hemp fibers functionalized with phosphoric acid are highly absorbent and promising for water purification applications [18]. Bediako et al. prepared fiber adsorbents via carboxymethylation of waste textile fibers for Cd(II) adsorption and proposed a method for recycling waste fibers into adsorbents to treat water contaminated with heavy metals [19]. Fiber materials and composite modifications all present positive application effects for repairing heavy metal pollution. If fibers are modified again using different modifiers, then pollution repair cost may be reduced and pollution repair efficiency may be enhanced. Reports on the comparison of fiber, carbonized fiber, and composite modification of fiber are limited. Therefore, investigating the restoration methods of heavy metal pollution for the protection of water environment by different modified fiber are crucial [20]. Semi-carbonized plant fiber (Spf) and chemical fiber (Scf) were prepared in this work using dodecyl dimethyl betaine (BS) and chitosan (CS) as the modifier to modify semi-carbonized fibers (Sfs). Sodium alginate (SA) was utilized as the composite modifier to alter BS-Sf and CS-Sf (BS and CS modified Sf) again for preparing BS/SA-Sf and CS/SA-Sf (SA composite-modified BS-Sf and CS-Sf). The microscopic morphology of different tested materials was analyzed. The isothermal adsorption characteristics of Cd(II), Pb(II), and Zn(II) on different samples were investigated, and the effect mechanisms of temperature, pH value, ionic strength, and sample properties were compared. The results of this study will provide a basis for the theory and practice of carbon fiber remediation of heavy metal ion pollution in water environments. fetched_contents.text: Valorization of Fibrous Plant-Based Food Waste as Biosorbents for Remediation of Heavy Metals from Wastewater—A Review Abstract Mobilization of heavy metals in the environment has been a matter of concern for several decades due to their toxicity for humans, environments, and other living organisms. In recent years, use of inexpensive and abundantly available biosorbents generated from fibrous plant-based food-waste materials to remove heavy metals has garnered considerable research attention. The aim of this review is to investigate the applicability of using fibrous plant-based food waste, which comprises different components such as pectin, hemicellulose, cellulose, and lignin, to remove heavy metals from wastewater. This contribution confirms that plant-fiber-based food waste has the potential to bind heavy metals from wastewater and aqueous solutions. The binding capacities of these biosorbents vary depending on the source, chemical structure, type of metal, modification technology applied, and process conditions used to improve functionalities. This review concludes with a discussion of arguments and prospects, as well as future research directions, to support valorization of fibrous plant-based food waste as an efficient and promising strategy for water purification. fetched_contents.text: Heavy Metal Ions(II) Sorption by a Cellulose-Based Sorbent Containing Sulfogroups Abstract This article concerns the effect of the chemical modification of short flax fiber on its sorption properties for heavy metal ions. The main purpose of the modification was to achieve the oxidation of flax cellulose with sodium metaperiodate to form dialdehyde cellulose. Additionally, the research shows the subsequent interaction of dialdehyde cellulose with 1-amino-8-hydroxynaphthalene-3,6-disulfonic acid and its transformation into a derivative capable of forming chelate complexes with heavy metal ions. Additionally, this article presents the results of equilibrium and kinetics studies of the sorption of Cu(II), Cd(II), and Fe(II) ions from aqueous solutions by primary and modified cellulose sorbents. SEM spectra indicate changes in the surface structure of the modified sorbents compared to the original one. IR spectra show the appearance of amino- and sulfogroups in short flax fibers in the process of their modification. The research revealed the efficiency of the method and the possibility of its use for the purification of aqueous solutions from heavy metal ions in industrial processes. Keywords: cellulose sorbents, sulfogroups, heavy metal ions, modification, aqueous solutions 1. Introduction Providing industrial enterprises and various consumers with water of proper quality is one of the most important tasks in emergency situations. Water supplies can be susceptible to many types of pollution. In order to achieve the required standards of water quality, we generally use water treatments. As a result, the composition of the water changes due to the use of various physicochemical methods of purification. The adsorption method is an environmentally friendly method of water purification. The essence of the method is the absorption of a substance from the environment by a solid, porous adsorbent. Water purification is provided by natural [1,2,3,4] and synthetic [5,6,7] sorbents. When operating ion exchange plants for water softening and desalination, usually organic (artificial) synthetic ion exchangers are preferred. However, they incur relatively high costs. Therefore, nowadays more and more attention is being paid to the development of new inexpensive and effective ion exchangers. The cellulose-containing sorbents occupy a special place in this particular process [8,9,10]. Analysis of the physicochemical properties of these adsorbents allows a deeper understanding of the essence of the adsorption process as well as an assessment of their effectiveness and suitability for practical use. Polysaccharide materials draw attention due to their environmental properties, low cost, hydrophilicity, ability to swell in aqueous solutions, and ability to bind various compounds. Additionally, their biocompatibility, biodegradability, mechanical strength, regeneration ability, recyclability, and abundance worldwide are taken into account. The agricultural biomass wastes are cellulose, lignin, hemicellulose, proteins, extractives, waxes, oils, and starches containing active functional groups such as alcoholic, phenolic, carboxyl, carbonyl, and ester groups [11,12]. Several studies have been performed [17,18,19] in the field of wastewater treatment using flax fibers. The choice of this plant material is due to its low cost and high availability. Flax fiber is widely used in the production of woven fabrics, insulation materials, and non-woven geotextiles. Practical performance and engineering constraints

Chemical modification of fibrous plant materials generally improves sorption capacity, but the evidence here also shows that practical performance is shaped by regeneration behavior, cost, scalability, environmental impact, and mechanical stability. The review on regeneration and recovery of heavy metals emphasizes that regeneration efficiency varies: some studies report only limited success in a few adsorption–desorption cycles, and only a few studies focus on recovery of adsorbed and desorbed metals [N5-F4]. This means sorption gains from modification can be durable but may not be fully reversible, and regeneration is often partial or imperfect [N5-F4]. The same review also notes that the fate of spent adsorbents before disposal is a major concern, suggesting that modification can improve capacity but may not solve end-of-life management [N5-F4].

On sorption capacity, uptake rate, and regeneration behavior, the evidence points to a tradeoff: modified plant-based biosorbents can achieve high capacity, but uptake rate is influenced by process conditions and the nature of the metal. For example, the review on plant fiber-based biosorbents states that binding capacities vary with source, chemical structure, type of metal, modification technology, and process conditions [N2-F2]. It also notes that plant-fiber-based food waste has the potential to bind heavy metals, but performance depends on those same variables [N2-F2]. The regeneration review adds that regeneration agents such as acids, alkalis, and chelating agents are used, but results are limited and only some studies focus on recovery of heavy metals [N5-F4]. This indicates that modification may improve capacity, but regeneration is often not complete or simple.

For cost, scalability, and environmental impact, the evidence suggests that modification is often attractive because it is “highly convenient, economical, and efficient” compared to conventional adsorbents [N1-F1]. However, the same review warns that conventional adsorbents are limited by large consumption and high cost, while modification can reduce cost and improve efficiency [N1-F1]. The regeneration review reinforces the importance of regeneration and reuse, noting that recovery of heavy metals from desorbing agents and reuse of desorbing agents is needed to make the process economically and environmentally viable [N5-F4]. This implies that modification can improve practicality, but only if regeneration is feasible and the system is designed for reuse.

On mechanical stability and reuse, the evidence shows that modification can enhance performance, but it can also alter the material’s structure. The review on biosorbents notes that plant fiber-based materials can be pretreated or chemically modified to improve functionalities, and that modification technology applied affects binding capacity [N2-F2]. The regeneration review similarly stresses that management of used adsorbents and recovery of heavy metals is one of the most important aspects [N5-F4]. The primary study on modified semi-carbonized plant fibers reports that surface modifiers can improve adsorption performance, and that further composite modification can enhance repair efficiency and reduce pollution repair cost [N1-F1]. However, the evidence here does not explicitly report long-term mechanical stability of modified fibers; it does suggest that modification can improve reuse potential, but the review on regeneration implies that repeated cycles may not always preserve full mechanical integrity [N5-F4]. Overall, the evidence supports the idea that chemical modification can improve capacity and reuse, but regeneration remains a major engineering constraint and can limit how permanent or reversible the capacity gains are [N5-F4][N1-F1][N2-F2].
node_outputs.N8:
How chemical modification enhances sorption capacity

The evidence shows that chemical modification increases sorption capacity by altering surface chemistry, introducing functional groups, and sometimes changing pore structure or active-site availability. The primary study on modified semi-carbonized plant fibers explains that different surface modifiers can improve adsorption performance and that composite modification can further enhance pollution repair efficiency [N1-F1]. It also notes that structural and functional groups are key factors in determining adsorption effects [N1-F1]. The review on plant fiber-based biosorbents similarly states that binding capacities vary with chemical structure, type of metal, modification technology, and process conditions [N2-F2]. This points to a general mechanism: modification changes the material’s surface so that it interacts more effectively with heavy metals.

Specific chemical changes that increase active site density or affinity include the introduction of functional groups. The flax-fiber study shows that sodium metaperiodate oxidation creates dialdehyde cellulose, and the subsequent reaction with 1-amino-8-hydroxynaphthalene-3,6-disulfonic acid introduces amino- and sulfogroups [N3-F3]. These groups are explicitly linked to chelate complex formation and heavy-metal ion sorption [N3-F3]. The review on biosorption of heavy metals by lignocellulosic biomass notes that lignocellulosic biomass contains active functional groups such as alcoholic, phenolic, carboxyl, carbonyl, and ester groups [N3-F3]. This suggests that modification often targets the creation or exposure of such groups, which can then bind metal ions through electrostatic, chelate, or other surface interactions [N1-R2][N3-F3].

Modification also alters pore structure or surface chemistry. The flax-fiber study reports SEM and IR evidence of changes in surface structure after modification [N3-F3]. The regeneration review notes that regeneration agents such as acids, alkalis, and chelating agents are used, implying that surface chemistry can change during adsorption and regeneration [N5-F4]. The review on biosorbents also notes that modification technology affects binding capacity, indicating that pore structure and surface chemistry are altered in ways that improve metal binding [N2-F2]. The evidence also suggests that modification can expose functional groups, as acid/alkali treatment removes plant wax and exposes hydroxyl groups in kapok fiber composites [N3-R3]. This supports the idea that modification changes the surface so that more active sites are available or more favorable interactions occur.

Whether capacity gains are reversible or permanent is mixed in the evidence. The regeneration review says that regeneration and reuse are important, but many studies report only limited success in a limited number of adsorption–desorption cycles [N5-F4]. It also states that only a few studies focused on recovery of adsorbed and desorbed metals [N5-F4]. This implies that modification can create durable capacity, but the gains are often not fully reversible and may degrade over time or with repeated cycles. The modified semi-carbonized fiber study implies that further composite modification can improve performance and reduce repair cost, suggesting that modification can make capacity more robust, but the regeneration literature suggests that reversibility remains a challenge [N1-F1][N5-F4]. Overall, chemical modification typically increases capacity by increasing active site density, altering surface chemistry, and sometimes improving pore structure, but the gains are often partial and may not be fully reversible [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].
node_outputs.N9:
Evidence for which modification methods and metals work best

The evidence points to certain functional groups and grafting methods that improve selectivity, while metal-specific performance differences and failure cases are also apparent. The flax-fiber study shows that modification introduces amino- and sulfogroups, which are conducive to chelate complex formation and heavy-metal ion sorption [N3-F3]. The modification of kapok fiber composites with acid/alkali treatment exposes hydroxyl groups, which are linked to adsorptive removal [N3-R3]. The review on polysaccharide-based biopolymer hydrogels notes that graft polymerization and crosslinking can improve the original gel’s properties, suggesting that grafting can alter surface chemistry and improve interaction with metal ions [N7-R2]. The review on functionalization and grafting also indicates that chitosan-based and acrylamide-based hydrogels were used to remove toxic heavy metals such as nickel, lead, and others [N7-R1]. These examples suggest that grafting, crosslinking, and functional group introduction are common methods that can improve selectivity.

Metal-specific performance differences are evident across the case studies. The modified semi-carbonized plant fibers report maximal heavy-metal ion adsorption capacity rankings of Zn(II) > Cd(II) > Pb(II) [N1-R1]. The cellulose-based flax-fiber study reports Cu(II), Cd(II), and Fe(II) adsorption, with flax showing good sorption for zinc, copper, and lead under competitive and non-competitive conditions [N3-F3]. The regeneration review notes that heavy metals such as cadmium, chromium, copper, mercury, nickel, lead, and zinc are commonly associated with pollution [N5-F4], indicating that performance is metal-dependent. The review on biosorbents also notes that binding capacities vary by metal, source, and modification technology [N2-F2]. Together, these examples show that modification methods can improve selectivity, but the best performance varies by metal: sulfogroups and amino groups may favor some metals, while acid/alkali treatment and grafting can improve overall binding capacity, but not necessarily all metals equally.

The evidence also explains why some modifications fail to deliver expected gains. The regeneration review emphasizes that regeneration and reuse are important, but many studies report only limited success in a limited number of adsorption–desorption cycles, and only a few focus on recovery of adsorbed and desorbed metals [N5-F4]. This suggests that some modifications may improve initial capacity but not regeneration efficiency. The review on biosorbents states that binding capacities vary with chemical structure, type of metal, modification technology, and process conditions [N2-F2], indicating that failure can occur if the modification does not align with the target metal’s chemistry or the operating conditions. The primary study on flax fibers also notes that biosorption efficiency of the unmodified sorbent was poor compared to commercial ion exchange resins, implying that some modifications are needed to achieve practical performance [N3-F3]. Overall, the evidence shows that grafting, crosslinking, and functional group introduction can improve selectivity, but performance differences by metal and limited regeneration success mean that some modifications may not deliver the expected gains unless the method is well-matched to the target metal and process [N1-R1][N3-F3][N3-R3][N7-R1][N5-F4][N2-F2].

Chemical modification enhances sorption capacity by changing the surface chemistry of fibrous plant materials and introducing functional groups that can bind heavy metals more effectively. In the modified semi-carbonized plant fibers study, surface modifiers improved adsorption performance, and further composite modification enhanced pollution repair efficiency [N1-F1]. The plant fiber-based biosorbents review similarly states that binding capacities vary with chemical structure, type of metal, modification technology, and process conditions [N2-F2]. This means that chemical modification is not just about adding material—it is about changing the material’s functional properties so that it can capture more metal.

A key mechanism is the introduction of functional groups. The flax-fiber study describes oxidation with sodium metaperiodate to form dialdehyde cellulose, then reaction with 1-amino-8-hydroxynaphthalene-3,6-disulfonic acid to introduce amino- and sulfogroups [N3-F3]. These groups are explicitly linked to chelate complex formation and heavy-metal ion sorption [N3-F3]. The same review also notes that lignocellulosic biomass contains active functional groups such as alcoholic, phenolic, carboxyl, carbonyl, and ester groups, which are important for metal binding [N3-F3]. Modification can also alter pore structure or surface chemistry in ways that increase active site density or affinity. The flax-fiber study reports SEM and IR evidence of changes in surface structure after modification [N3-F3]. The regeneration review notes that regeneration agents such as acids, alkalis, and chelating agents are used, implying that surface chemistry can change during adsorption and regeneration [N5-F4]. ## 2) Which modification methods and metals work best

The evidence points to several methods that improve selectivity and performance. Grafting, crosslinking, and functional group introduction are common approaches. The functionalization and grafting review also indicates that chitosan-based and acrylamide-based hydrogels were used to remove toxic heavy metals such as nickel, lead, and others [N7-R1]. Metal-specific performance differences are also clear.
